correctness.rationale: The constant-speed parameter is uniform under arclength sampling. Sorting gives density 6/(2π)^3; changing to the two positive gaps and the first parameter has unit Jacobian. Direct chord scalar products give the three sign tests in the proof. The middle one is ab(H-c²). For a+b>π, strict concavity of log(sin x/x) on (0,π) maximizes H at equal gaps at each fixed sum. The continuous boundary values also lie strictly below the unique interior maximum: at a zero gap use strict concavity extended at 0, and at total gap 2π the best value is h(π)<h(t*). For smaller totals up to π, H is nonpositive. The derivative of log h is G, strictly decreasing from +∞ to -2/π, so the root is unique. At the maximizing gaps both end dot products remain positive, including at c=c*, and all three are positive on a neighborhood when c<c*. At and above the threshold the middle sign forbids strict acuteness. Differentiation gives the stated Hessian eigenvalues md and me, positive since sin(t*/2)<t*/2; the unique compact-domain maximum localizes the near-critical event at distance O(sqrt(m-c²)). Taylor expansion and dominated convergence give ellipse area 2π/(m sqrt(de)) in the rescaled variables and the limiting weight 2π-2t*. This produces the stated coefficient and joint independent uniform limit for the first parameter. Bounded independent bisection on G and evaluation of the Hessian expression reproduced t*=2.670778089087041, c*=0.6874374448319006 and C=0.9898164405674238. The supplied numerical script was inspected, not executed; the root replay supplies no proof of global maximization or of the limit.

value.rationale: This gives a sharp geometric boundary for a natural sampling measure on a standard space curve. The exact onset coefficient and conditional ellipse say how acute configurations disappear, not just where extinction occurs. The middle-angle reduction ties the existence threshold and the probability law together. The value is for the specified one turn and strict Euclidean angles, not a monotonicity statement, a theorem for all supports, or an elementary closed expression for the full probability.
